First Warn Forecast

Thursday, August 13, 2026

Dangerous Heat Continues
A Few Strong Storms Possible North
Relief Arrives Early Next Week

Dangerous heat and humidity remain the main weather story across the region today and will continue into at least Saturday. Temperatures will again climb into the lower and middle 90s, with some locations along and south of I-70 reaching the middle and upper 90s.

Dew points will remain in the lower to middle 70s, making it feel much hotter than the actual air temperature. Heat index values will generally range from 100 to 105 degrees during the afternoon.

Cloud cover and nearby thunderstorms may hold temperatures down somewhat across northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois, but the humidity will remain high. Even where temperatures are a few degrees cooler, it will still feel very muggy and uncomfortable.

The large ridge of high pressure responsible for this prolonged stretch of heat will continue building northward through the end of the week and into the weekend. That means there is very little opportunity for meaningful heat relief before Sunday.

Continue to take precautions during the hottest part of the day. Drink plenty of water, limit extended outdoor activity when possible, and check on anyone who may be especially vulnerable to the heat.

Isolated Storms Today

Radar early this morning shows isolated showers and thunderstorms near the I-70 corridor and around the St. Louis metropolitan area.

A stationary front draped across the region is helping provide enough lift for these scattered showers and thunderstorms. As southerly winds increase and the upper-level ridge strengthens, that boundary is expected to slowly lift northward through the day.

Additional isolated showers and thunderstorms may develop along the front as it moves north.

Meanwhile, a larger area of thunderstorms across eastern Nebraska will move through Iowa today. Similar to what we saw Wednesday, that system will travel along the northern edge of the ridge and could eventually send an outflow boundary southward into northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois.

That boundary could provide enough lift to generate a few thunderstorms across our northern counties this afternoon and evening.

The Storm Prediction Center has placed portions of northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois in a Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms.

The primary severe weather concern will be damaging wind gusts. Any stronger storm could produce a powerful downdraft capable of bringing strong winds to the surface.

The overall severe weather threat is lower than what we experienced Wednesday. The strengthening ridge is producing more sinking air across the region, which should limit the amount and intensity of thunderstorm development.

Most locations will likely remain dry, but any storm that manages to develop could briefly become strong.

Friday Stays Hot

Little changes Friday.

Temperatures will once again reach the lower to middle 90s across much of the region, with the best chance of highs reaching or exceeding 95 degrees along and south of I-70.

Humidity remains high, with dew points again in the lower and middle 70s. Heat index values will likely reach 100 to 105 degrees during the afternoon.

Areas farther north may see slightly lower temperatures because of additional cloud cover associated with nearby thunderstorms.

Unfortunately, the combination of heat and humidity will remain dangerous, particularly during the afternoon and early evening.

Heat Holds On Saturday

The hot and humid pattern continues Saturday.

Forecast guidance shows a high probability of temperatures reaching at least 95 degrees along and south of I-70. Dew points will remain elevated, keeping the heat index well above the actual temperature.

Saturday may end up being another day where heat index values approach or exceed 100 degrees in many locations.

There is also the possibility of another thunderstorm complex developing north of the region Saturday night into Sunday. The setup could be similar to what we have seen the last couple of days, with storms traveling around the northern edge of the ridge.

If that happens, cloud cover and an outflow boundary could move into portions of the area and hold temperatures down somewhat Sunday.

That possibility, combined with uncertainty regarding the timing of the approaching cold front, makes Sunday's temperature forecast a little more complicated.

A Cold Front Finally Brings Relief

The good news continues to be what we see developing late Sunday into Monday.

Forecast guidance remains in good agreement that a cold front will move through the region as the upper-level ridge begins to weaken and shift.

Winds behind the front will turn more northerly, allowing cooler and noticeably less humid air to move into Missouri and Illinois.

Temperatures should return closer to seasonal averages Monday and Tuesday, and the drop in humidity may be even more noticeable than the temperature change.

After several days of dew points in the 70s and heat index values above 100 degrees, even a return to more typical August weather will feel significantly better.

How long that relief lasts remains uncertain.

Forecast guidance becomes much less consistent by the middle of next week. Some models rebuild the ridge and bring another surge of heat and humidity northward, while others keep the ridge farther southwest and allow additional cooler air to move into the region.

That uncertainty is reflected in a fairly large spread in forecast temperatures by Wednesday and beyond.

For now, the message remains straightforward. Dangerous heat and humidity continue through Saturday, a few strong thunderstorms are possible mainly across northeastern Missouri and west-central Illinois today, and our best opportunity for meaningful relief arrives with a cold front Sunday into Monday.

First. Accurate. Trusted.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
